analysis.one_liner: Creates government-funded jobs in high-unemployment communities, paid for by taxing stock and futures trades.
analysis.headline: A jobs bill with 52 Democratic cosponsors received no committee vote and no floor action, and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a Full Employment National Trust Fund filled by a new 0.25% tax on securities and futures transactions, collected from the exchanges where trades occur. The money would fund direct jobs for the long-term unemployed and low-income workers in distressed communities, on projects like repairing schools, restoring vacant properties, staffing child care and Head Start, and maintaining parks, at wages and hours set by the bill. It would also put minority-serving community organizations on state and local workforce boards and convene a national employment conference. It never advanced past committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Unemployed and underemployed people in distressed communities. The bill requires that hires be out of work at least 26 weeks, or at least 30 days and low-income, and that at least 35 percent of workers come from the targeted low-income group. Jobs must pay at least 30 hours a week for at least 12 months at wages matching similar existing work, with construction workers paid local prevailing wages, and at least 80 percent of project funding going to wages, benefits, and support services like child care. Community organizations and local governments doing the projects also gain funding, and workforce programs get a dedicated revenue stream.

how_it_helps.text: Creates direct public jobs for the long-term unemployed in communities with high poverty, foreclosures, and vacancy, targeting projects like school repair, blight remediation, emergency food programs, and Head Start staffing [S3].

Sets job quality standards: at least 12 months of employment at 30 hours per week, pay equal to similar existing work, prevailing wages on construction, and 80 percent of funding for wages, benefits, and support services including child care [S3].
Guards against displacement: funded workers cannot replace existing employees or furloughed workers, and cannot work where a union contract covers the same work without the union's consent [S3].

Funds the program with a 0.25% tax on securities and futures transactions, paid by the trading facilities where the trades occur, so the cost falls on trading volume rather than on workers or general taxpayers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Investors and the securities and futures trading industry, through the 0.25% tax on the value of each covered transaction, paid by the exchanges and trading facilities. The tax would apply to stocks, bonds, and futures transactions under SEC or CFTC jurisdiction.

drawbacks.text: A transaction tax raises trading costs for everyone who invests, including mutual fund and retirement account holders, and trading may move to foreign exchanges to avoid it; the bill collects the tax only from US trading facilities, which could shift activity overseas rather than raise the projected revenue.

The program is contingent on annual appropriations and on the Federal Reserve chairman certifying the economy is not at full employment, so it is neither automatic nor guaranteed, and the jobs it creates are temporary, defined projects rather than permanent employment [S3].

Requiring 26 weeks of unemployment to qualify can leave newly laid-off workers without help and can create incentives for people near eligibility to wait for program jobs instead of taking available work.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For communities with chronic unemployment, the bill offered well-paid temporary work with real protections against displacing existing employees, funded by a tax on high-volume trading. The serious tradeoffs are that the transaction tax raises costs for ordinary investors' retirement savings and risks pushing trading offshore, and the jobs are temporary rather than permanent. The design is more careful than most jobs bills, but the revenue and employment effects depend on assumptions that were never tested because the bill never advanced.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to two committees the day it was introduced; one sent it to a subcommittee three weeks later, and neither committee ever took further action, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers introduced the bill on March 2, 2011, and 52 House Democrats cosponsored it [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Education and the Workforce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction [S5].

On March 21, 2011, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Higher Education and Workforce Training; that was the last action of any kind in the record, and no markup, vote, or floor consideration ever occurred [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Securities and futures trading firms avoided the 0.25% transaction tax, and the Republican-led committees faced no obligation to act on a jobs program they did not advance. Unemployed workers in distressed communities got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Financial firms that avoided the trading tax

for.name: Rep. John Conyers, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 52 Democratic cosponsors.

for.name: 52 of 435 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored it.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote; sent the bill to a subcommittee on March 21, 2011, and took no further action.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the tax provision referred to it; the bill received no hearing or markup there in the record.

sides.party_line_note: All 52 cosponsors were Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat; the Republican-led committees took no action, and there was no floor vote to break down by party.

industries.note: The bill imposes a 0.25% tax on the value of every covered stock, bond, and futures transaction, collected from the exchanges and trading facilities. Trading firms and high-frequency traders bear the largest costs, and that cost is the funding source for the jobs program.
A transaction tax raises the cost of every trade, including trades inside mutual funds and retirement accounts, though smaller investors trade far less frequently than institutions.

industries.industry: Job training and workforce development providers
industries.note: The bill dedicates a third of the trust fund to Workforce Investment Act programs and requires 33 percent of funding to flow to training and employment services, giving workforce boards a new dedicated revenue stream.
The bill reserves a guaranteed share of state and local workforce board seats for their chief executives and makes them eligible grant recipients for the community jobs projects.
